_comment: ai-memory lifecycle hooks for DeepSeek Harness — EXAMPLE / TEMPLATE.
This file is a starting point, not something the plugin installs for you.
Replace every <PLACEHOLDER> below with your own paths, then point a row in
your profile's cordis.patch.yml at it (INSERT form — a bare `- id:` row only
overrides an existing loader and would be ignored for a new one):
- insert:
- id: hooks-ai-memory
name: '@deepseek-ai/dsh-hooks-claude-code'
config:
configPath: <ABSOLUTE PATH TO THIS FILE>
defaultTimeoutMs: 30000
The bridge reads this file ONCE at startup, so a change takes effect only
after DSH restarts.
WHY THIS LEGACY FILE IS HAND-WRITTEN:
Older ai-memory presets emit exec form - the binary in `command` and every flag
in a sibling `args` array. dsh-hooks-claude-code does not read `args` at
all: it keeps only `typeof hook.command === 'string'` and discards the rest.
Running the generated snippet therefore spawns ai-memory with no arguments,
which prints its help text and exits 1 - capture silently does nothing.
This is the LEGACY template: every capture command uses `claude-code`.
ai-memory >=3.2.0 now has a native `dsh` kind and first-party DSH support.
For native capture on those releases, replace --agent claude-code with
--agent dsh in ALL seven commands and restart DSH before a new session.
Do not use dsh with older ai-memory. Leave the plugin agentKind unset:
it reads each stored session's actual kind, preserving legacy backlog.
The manual commands below remain single strings for the bridge API.
DSH runs each command as:
pwsh -NoLogo -NoProfile -NonInteractive -Command <string>
which means ordinary PowerShell quoting works. On Windows, keep the `&`
call operator.
EVENTS: exactly the ones dsh-hooks-claude-code supports - SessionStart,
UserPromptSubmit, PreToolUse, PostToolUse, Stop, SubagentStart,
SubagentStop. ai-memory's own Claude Code preset also lists PreCompact and
SessionEnd; DSH fires neither, so they are omitted rather than registered as
dead entries. That missing SessionEnd is precisely why this plugin exists:
without `dsh-ai-memory`, a DSH session stays open in ai-memory forever and
never becomes a wiki page or a handoff.
PreToolUse is INCLUDED here (it records tool intent as its own observation),
but it is the first thing to delete if latency hurts: DSH awaits every hook
synchronously and has no async hook option (unlike Codex, whose `async: true`
takes a multi-second hook off the response path). ai-memory's claude-code
dialect answers `{}` for pre-tool-use, so it never grants or blocks a tool.
Measured on DSH 0.2.1-rc.2 / Windows: one hook costs ~0.5 s of shell startup
in isolation, but ~3 s end-to-end through DSH's subprocess runner, so
PreToolUse + PostToolUse add roughly 6 s per tool call. Remove PreToolUse to
halve that; PostToolUse is what actually records the tool result.
WHY Stop CHAINS `hook-drain`: ai-memory buffers each event into a spool file
and delivers it in a background drainer it spawns itself. Its native presets
trigger that drain on SessionEnd, and DSH never fires SessionEnd - so events
sat in the spool until the next SessionStart. Chaining the hidden but
documented-for-hooks `hook-drain` command makes delivery happen at the end of
every turn instead. Without it, recall in a new session is always one session
behind. Measured cost of the drain itself: ~40-80 ms.
SANDBOX: DSH runs hook commands through ctx.shell WITHOUT a session, so they
use the deployment-default policy rather than the session's mode. On DSH
0.2.1-rc.2 / Windows that default is `workspace-write`, whose ACL runner is
broken in the Electron build: every child dies STATUS_DLL_INIT_FAILED
(0xC0000142) after 6-9 s, capture records nothing, and the failure is silent.
Two working responses, either is enough:
a) set the deployment default to `danger-full-access` (the sandbox is then
skipped entirely: `pwsh-sandbox` returns before confinement), or
b) grant write on ai-memory's data directory to Everyone, which is what
ai-memory's own Windows launcher does for its spool.
Verify capture with `ai-memory status` - observations must rise while you
work. Do not trust "the hook is registered" as evidence of capture.
REPLACE <AI_MEMORY_EXE> with the full path to ai-memory.exe (Windows) or
ai-memory (Linux/macOS), and <AI_MEMORY_DATA_DIR> with your data directory:
Windows: %LOCALAPPDATA%\ai-memory
Linux:   ~/.local/share/ai-memory
macOS:   ~/Library/Application Support/ai-memory
On Linux/macOS the command string must use POSIX quoting instead, e.g.
"<AI_MEMORY_EXE>" --data-dir "<AI_MEMORY_DATA_DIR>" hook --event stop ...
